Article Title: Brazil's Snake Island is home to just two snake species, including one of the world's most venomous pit vipers
Article Text:
Image: Left/Golden lancehead (Bothrops insularis)/Right/Dipsas albifrons (Sauvage's snail-eating snake)/AI Generated

Brazil 's Snake Island has only two snake species, one among the deadliest

1. Golden lancehead (Bothrops insularis)

Image: AI Generated

2. Dipsas albifrons (Sauvage's snail-eating snake)

Image: AI Generated

Why are there so many snakes on the island?

Why is Snake Island closed to the public?

About 33 kilometres off the coast of São Paulo lies Ilha da Queimada Grande, better known as Snake Island. Shrouded in myths of deadly encounters and pirate treasure, the island has earned a fearsome reputation as one of the most snake-infested places on Earth. While stories often claim there is "one snake per square metre", modern estimates suggest the island is home to around 2,000 to 4,000 snakes spread across its 43-hectare landscape. Despite its fearsome reputation, only two snake species are known to inhabit the island: the critically endangered golden lancehead (Bothrops insularis) and the harmless Sauvage's snail-eating snake (Dipsas albifrons). Nearly all of the island's snakes are golden lanceheads, a highly specialised species found nowhere else on Earth. According to Smithsonian Magazine, the island's extraordinary isolation has turned it into a living laboratory of evolution, where one of the world's rarest venomous snakes has adapted in remarkable ways.The undisputed ruler of Snake Island is the golden lancehead, a critically endangered pit viper that exists naturally only on Ilha da Queimada Grande. Around 11,000 years ago, rising sea levels isolated the island from mainland Brazil, trapping the ancestors of these snakes.Over thousands of generations, they evolved into a distinct species with unique adaptations.Unlike its mainland relatives, the golden lancehead feeds primarily on migratory birds rather than rodents. Birds can escape after being bitten, so the snake evolved exceptionally fast-acting venom capable of immobilising prey almost immediately. Smithsonian Magazine explains that this evolutionary pressure made the venom several times more potent than that of closely related mainland lanceheads, helping prevent wounded birds from flying away before dying.Despite its deadly reputation, researchers note that the snake is generally not aggressive towards humans. Because public access to the island is prohibited, documented bites are extremely rare. The greater concern today is not human safety, but the snake's survival, as illegal wildlife trafficking and habitat changes have contributed to declining populations. Discover Wildlife notes that a single illegally collected specimen can command tens of thousands of dollars on the black market, making conservation a major priority.Although Snake Island is best known for the golden lancehead, it is not the island's only snake. The Sauvage's snail-eating snake (Dipsas albifrons) also inhabits the island. Unlike the lancehead, this species is non-venomous and specialises in feeding on snails and slugs rather than birds or mammals. It is slender, nocturnal and poses no danger to people.Its presence highlights that Snake Island supports a more complex ecosystem than its fearsome reputation suggests. While the golden lancehead dominates the headlines, the snail-eater occupies an entirely different ecological niche, helping maintain balance within the island's invertebrate populations.The island's unusual snake density is the result of isolation and evolution rather than human intervention. With virtually no terrestrial predators and few competing reptiles, the golden lancehead population expanded over thousands of years. However, food remained scarce because there were no native mammals, forcing the snakes to specialise in hunting migratory birds that stop on the island during seasonal journeys. This unique food source shaped both their behaviour and the remarkable potency of their venom.The Brazilian government strictly controls access to Ilha da Queimada Grande. Only authorised researchers and, occasionally, Brazilian Navy personnel maintaining the automated lighthouse are permitted to visit. While the venomous snakes present obvious risks, the restrictions are equally important for protecting the critically endangered golden lancehead from disturbance and illegal collection.Today, Snake Island remains one of the world's most remarkable examples of island evolution. Home to just two native snake species, one of them among the planet's rarest and most specialised vipers, it continues to fascinate scientists studying evolution, venom biology and conservation, while reminding us how isolation can produce extraordinary forms of life.
Article Summary: Brazil's Snake Island has only two snake species, one among the world's deadliest. The island is home to around 2,000 to 4,000 snakes spread across its 43-hectare landscape. Nearly all of the island's snakes are golden lanceheads, a highly specialised species found nowhere else on Earth. Despite its fearsome reputation, documented bites are extremely rare.

Article Title: After 27 years and 18 desk moves, Jeff Dean is leaving Google; His ‘goodbye email’ explains why
Article Text:
Jeff Dean, Google's 30th employee and chief scientist, is leaving after 27 years to lead AI startup Discovery Loop.

What Jeff Dean built at Google, and what he wants to build next

Jeff Dean's goodbye email to Google, in full

Subject: Thank you and farewell

Hi everyone,

It has been an absolute pleasure to work with you and to help build some of the most widely used and impactful products of all time. As a kid, I dreamed of helping build software that would be used by many people, and Google now has thirteen products used by more than a billion people (amazing!). Our work has had a tremendous impact in the world, and I have been lucky enough to collaborate and form friendships with many colleagues whom I deeply admire, respect, and enjoy.

It still brings me joy every time I see people out in the world using our products to find information, handle email, translate something, watch videos, learn new things, navigate and understand the physical world, browse the web, use their phone, run large-scale computations on our infrastructure, ride in an autonomous vehicle, or perform complex tasks with the help of our AI systems. I hope you all share this sense of joy, because it is a shared accomplishment!

My longtime friends and collaborators Sanjay Ghemawat, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le and I have been excitedly discussing how AI can help discover new things with the right kinds of automated loops.

It's a big step, but we've decided to leave Google to co-found Discovery Loop, a new public benefit corporation whose mission is to automate machine learning, science, and engineering to accelerate discoveries and progress.

Ambitious as it sounds, we believe this approach can make meaningful progress against many of the NAE Grand Challenge problems (nae.edu/20782/grand-challenges-project), and we are excited about trying something new, in a smaller setting. Sundar and Alphabet have been very understanding and are helping to support us along with outside investors. We leave with the belief that Google and Gemini are extremely well positioned for amazing impact in the future and we will all be cheering you on from outside!

I have deeply enjoyed collaborating and starting many different kinds of projects here over the last 27 years, and I will miss many aspects of this. Some of the projects and memories I will cherish include:

Working on multiple generations of Google Search as we increased our index size 100X, our queries served / sec 1000X, and our update frequency for the index by 10,000X over a few-year period

Creating the first Google Ads system and later creating and launching Google Content Ads

Helping to launch Google News and Google Translate

Working on infrastructure like MapReduce, BigTable, Spanner, DistBelief, TensorFlow, and Pathways with an awesome set of people

Starting the TPU program and working on other exciting hardware projects with talented colleagues

Doing research with many others on unsupervised learning, model distillation, mixture-of-experts model architectures, word2vec, neural architecture search, RL for ASIC design, AI for health care, and working on multiple generations of Large Language Models (LLMs)

Seeing the awesome work that people in Google Brain and Google Research did over many years when I was lucky enough to manage these organizations

Starting the Gemini effort with Oriol Vinyals as co-tech-leads and working with an amazing team on multiple generations of Gemini and Gemma

Biking to offsites in Monterey

The "Run or Else…" group runs over the last few years

Changing offices 18 times, and visiting 29 Google offices across five continents (did you know that with a Google badge, you can make a cappuccino in more than 100 cities around the world?)

Most importantly, feeling lucky and inspired getting to work amongst such a wonderful and talented group of colleagues

To the many, many people with whom I have worked over the years, I apologize for this impersonal email rather than a face-to-face chat: I didn't want you all to find out through second- or third-hand gossip and it was impractical to tell everyone in a more personal way all at once.

I will be at Google through tomorrow, August 6th. If you're in Mountain View and are so inclined, please stop by my desk and say goodbye in person tomorrow, or drop me a reply to this email. There will be a [remainder redacted in the shared screenshot]

All the best!

-Jeff

Jeff Dean's farewell note to Google runs long, and the most telling part isn't about AI at all. It's a list. Wedged between scaling Google Search's index 100X and starting the TPU program, he mentions biking to offsites in Monterey, a group run called "Run or Else…", changing offices 18 times, and the fact that a Google badge gets you a cappuccino in more than 100 cities. Twenty-seven years, reduced to bullet points he clearly enjoyed writing.The news underneath the nostalgia: Thursday, August 6 is his last day. Dean, chief scientist at Google DeepMind and one of the very few engineers whose work touches nearly every layer of Google's stack, is leaving to co-found Discovery Loop, a public benefit corporation, with Sanjay Ghemawat, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le. He joined in 1999, when the company had 25 employees. He leaves it at 190,000-plus.CEO Sundar Pichai 's send-off for Jeff Dean drew the same arc: over 27 years, he said, Dean and Ghemawat drove some of Google's most significant technology transitions, from its early search infrastructure to the neural networks that built the modern AI era. "On a personal note, it's been a privilege to work alongside Jeff and Sanjay," Pichai wrote, adding that Google will keep collaborating with the new startup as a founding investor and Cloud partner.Dean’s résumé is most of modern Google. He wrote the first Ads system, helped launch News and Translate, and with Ghemawat designed MapReduce, BigTable and Spanner—systems that became the template for how Amazon and Meta handled global traffic. The two are the only Google employees ever named senior fellow, the company's highest technical honour. Then came 2011 and Google Brain, the research lab Dean built that pushed the entire industry toward AI. Its early hires included Le and Vinyals, the same two men now following him out.That's the quiet irony here. Brain's researchers helped pioneer the technology behind today's chatbots, and Google was slow to act on it. After ChatGPT landed in late 2022, the company folded Brain into DeepMind, and Dean and Vinyals were put on Gemini. His profile inside Google appeared to shrink as Sergey Brin returned and took hold of the AI push.Discovery Loop is an attempt to skip the bureaucracy entirely. The four want to build AI that improves itself with little human input—recursive self-improvement—then point the same machinery at chip design, drug discovery and materials science. Dean's argument is that the experimental loop has always been human-intensive and doesn't have to be. Seed funding comes from Radical Ventures, Khosla Ventures and Alphabet itself, which has also agreed to supply compute for at least a year. It's structured as a public benefit corporation, like Anthropic and OpenAI, and Dean says it may make calls that aren't in the company's purest financial interests.The note ends with an apology for being an email. He didn't want people hearing it as second-hand gossip, he writes, and invites anyone in Mountain View to stop by his desk. That's the tell. A man who spent 27 years building systems for a billion users at a time signed off worrying about how a few thousand colleagues would find out.
Article Summary: Jeff Dean, Google's 30th employee and chief scientist, is leaving after 27 years to lead AI startup Discovery Loop. Dean's goodbye email to Google, in full: "It has been an absolute pleasure to work with you and to help build some of the most widely used and impactful products"

Article Title: Meta launches Muse Code, its first AI coding agent to rival OpenAI and Anthropic
Article Text:
Meta launches Muse Code, its first AI coding agent to rival OpenAI and Anthropic

What is Meta Muse Code and how does it work

Muse Spark 1.2 powers Meta's new coding agent

Meta has launched its first AI coding agent, Muse Code, as the tech giant steps up its push to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic. Currently released in beta, Muse Code is a terminal-based coding agent powered by Meta’s new Muse Spark 1.2 model. Announcing the new models, the company says that it can handle complex software engineering tasks across large code repositories, including planning changes, writing code and checking whether the results work correctly.Unlike a basic AI coding assistant that mainly suggests or generates pieces of code, Muse Code is claimed to be designed to work as an agent capable of carrying out longer and more complicated software engineering tasks. According to Meta, Muse Code uses a main AI agent along with multiple specialised background agents. These background agents remain active throughout a coding session and can gather information, work on next steps and decide when they need to report their findings to the main agent.Meta says this approach can help the coding agent solve difficult problems faster while requiring less intervention from developers.The company says it has also designed Muse Code to handle long-running jobs. Every model call, tool run, approval and code edit is stored in a local event log. If the agent crashes or stops unexpectedly, it can restart from exactly where it left off instead of beginning the task again.Muse Code also comes with built-in skills. The /plan command can create a plan that requires user approval, while /grill can test that plan for possible problems. Another command, /goal, directs the agent to keep working towards completing a specified objective.At the centre of Muse Code is Muse Spark 1.2, Meta's latest AI model and a coding-focused update to Muse Spark 1.1. Meta says it increased the amount of training compute devoted to coding tasks while also expanding the variety of training environments used to develop the new model.The company claims Muse Spark 1.2 improves code generation, complex debugging, understanding of large codebases and end-to-end developer workflows. It has also been trained for long-running coding jobs, including generating entire repositories and working on large projects.
Article Summary: Muse Code is a terminal-based coding agent powered by Meta’s new Muse Spark 1.2 model. It can handle complex software engineering tasks across large code repositories, including planning changes, writing code and checking whether the results work correctly.

Article Title: UltraProlink launches Snap-Z, a DSLR-style magnetic smartphone grip
Article Text: Home-grown consumer tech brand UltraProlink has launched the Snap-Z Grip, a compact magnetic smartphone camera grip with a DSLR camera style magnetic grip. In a press release, the company said that the gadget is designed for content creators, travellers, vloggers. It combines an ergonomic grip, intuitive traditional-style controls, a Mag-Safe-style magnetic attachment and a detachable Bluetooth shutter. The UltraProlink Snap-Z Grip is available for Rs 1,999 on UltraProlink.com and Amazon.in.“The thoughtful design helps reduce hand fatigue while improving stability for reels, travel videos, product photography and everyday shooting in both portrait and landscape orientations,” the company said.The Snap-Z comes with a Mag-Safe-style magnetic mount that snaps securely onto compatible iPhones and magnetic cases. The magnetic metal ring included in the box extends compatibility to Android smartphones and other non-magnetic devices. This makes the Grip a versatile accessory that works with almost any smartphone.The firm also has provided a metal ring in the box for non-magnetic phones. Its detachable Bluetooth shutter functions as a tactile camera button while attached to the grip and doubles as a wireless remote with a range of up to 10m, ideal for selfies, group photos, tripod shots and hands-free videos.It pairs instantly with both Android and iPhone devices and works directly with the native camera app without requiring any additional software.The grip features one-handed controls with a responsive shutter button, zoom toggle and mode-switching support. The grip weighs 109g and can slip easily into a pocket, sling bag or backpack. Its dual-sided magnetic design also supports compatible accessories such as ring lights, to expand your mobile shooting setup with ease.Commenting on the launch, Pankaj Mirchandani, Founder & CEO, UltraProlink said: “Smartphones are the world’s most-used cameras, but holding one steady shouldn’t be this hard. UltraProlink’s Snap-Z Grip is a single compact accessory that brings the comfort of a DSLR-like ergonomic grip to every smartphone. It makes every shot possible with one hand, feel steadier, more comfortable and more enjoyable”
Article Summary: The Snap-Z comes with a Mag-Safe-style magnetic mount that snaps securely onto compatible iPhones and magnetic cases. The grip features one-handed controls with a responsive shutter button, zoom toggle and mode-switching support. Its detachable Bluetooth shutter functions as a tactile camera button while attached to the grip and doubles as a wireless remote.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: CUSAT scientists develop stem cell-like fish cell line for advanced research
Article Text:
Kochi

:





Researchers at the National Centre for Aquatic Animal Health (NCAAH) of Cusat have developed a stem cell-like cell line from fish embryos that can survive and grow in the laboratory for a long time. Scientists say the achievement is a major step forward for fish biotechnology research in India.The research was led by Jayesh Puthumana, assistant professor at NCAAH, along with research scholar Aswathi . Their findings have been accepted for publication in the international journal Fish Physiology and Biochemistry.The new cell line, named ATES1, behaves like stem cells and can grow without the support of feeder cells, making it easier to use for research.According to Puthumana, ATES1 can help scientists study fish diseases, the immune system, genetics, gene editing and test new drugs and vaccines. It could also support research on cultivated fish meat.The study also showed that the cell line can be genetically modified efficiently using a virus-free method, making it useful for future biotechnology and cell biology research.The research, supported by the department of biotechnology (DBT), govt of India, took more than four-and-a-half years to complete and is expected to open new opportunities in fish biotechnology research.
Article Summary: Scientists say the achievement is a major step forward for fish biotechnology research in India. The new cell line, named ATES1, behaves like stem cells and can grow without the support of feeder cells. The study also showed that the cell line can be genetically modified efficiently using a virus-free method.

Article Title: A 45,000-year-old crystal tool found in France suggests Neanderthals chose beauty as well as practicality
Article Text:
A remarkable find in France reveals a 45,000-year-old Neanderthal quartz scraper that changes the narrative around these ancient beings. This tool, crafted from rare rock crystal, highlights that Neanderthals had an appreciation for aesthetics and craftsmanship, challenging the notion of them as mere primitive beings. The sophistication in its creation suggests a deeper cultural understanding and skillful manipulation of their environment, offering insights into Neanderthal life and artistry.

45,000-year-old Neanderthal quartz scraper highlights unusual stone tool technology in France

Neanderthal rock crystal tools show careful material selection

PC: Ministère de la Culture

Neanderthal creativity beyond old stereotypes

Ancient tool revealed the complexity of Neanderthal culture

A small artefact with a long scientific legacy

A small piece of translucent quartz discovered in a French cave nearly a century ago has continued to reshape the way scientists view Neanderthals. The object, a carefully worked rock crystal scraper, was not made from the materials these prehistoric toolmakers usually relied upon. Instead, someone selected a rare, visually striking stone and transformed it into a practical tool. Its careful manufacture has prompted archaeologists to reconsider how Neanderthals chose raw materials and whether appearance influenced certain tool-making decisions. Found among other quartz artefacts in the Dordogne region, the discovery challenged early assumptions that Neanderthals lacked creativity or an appreciation for unusual materials. Today, the artefact offers a glimpse into how function and visual appeal may have existed together in Neanderthal craftsmanship.The rock crystal scraper comes from Abri des Merveilles, an archaeological site in southwestern France’s Dordogne region. Reportedly, the cave became significant after American archaeologists uncovered a group of unusual quartz tools there in 1924.As per the 1931 American School of Prehistoric Research bulletin , the excavation was led by George MacCurdy from the institution now associated with Harvard University.Among the finds was a transparent, yellow-tinted piece of microcrystalline quartz that had been shaped into a tool. The artefact is now held by France’s National Archaeological Museum.Unlike many Neanderthal tools made from flint or chert, this object was created from rock crystal, a material that behaves differently when fractured. Flint was often preferred because it produced predictable sharp edges, making it reliable for cutting and scraping tasks. Quartz required more skill and judgement, as its structure made shaping it less straightforward.The cave also contained small fragments of quartz left behind during production, suggesting the tool was likely made at the site rather than carried there after completion.The presence of rock crystal tools at Neanderthal sites has long attracted attention because the material appears to have been selected for more than just its usefulness.The scraper may have served a practical purpose, possibly as a combination scraping and pointed implement. Yet its clear appearance and unusual colour raised questions about why Neanderthals chose this stone when other materials were easier to work.According to Harvard University, American School of Prehistoric Research, the quartz may have come from deposits connected to waterways near the Vézère River, a tributary of the Dordogne. The exact age of the Abri des Merveilles layers remains uncertain, but archaeological evidence suggests the tools were created somewhere around 45,000 years ago.For much of the early 20th century, Neanderthals were often portrayed as primitive and lacking the abilities associated with modern humans. According to the 1931 bulletin, these ideas were heavily influenced by interpretations of Neanderthal fossils, including the remains of an elderly individual from La Chapelle-aux-Saints in France.The individual had suffered from severe arthritis, but early interpretations focused on physical differences and helped create the inaccurate image of Neanderthals as crude, almost animal-like beings.MacCurdy’s interpretation of the rock crystal tools offered a different perspective. He argued that the choice of material showed an awareness of shape, colour and quality. In his view, the tools indicated that Neanderthals were capable of recognising aesthetic qualities even while making objects for everyday use.He did not describe them as artists in the same way as later human societies are understood to have been, but he suggested that they possessed a sense of visual appreciation.When the quartz tools were first studied, evidence of Neanderthal symbolic behaviour was far more limited than it is today. Archaeologists had not yet uncovered many of the examples now associated with Neanderthal creativity, including possible pigment use, engravings and decorative objects.Later discoveries and advances in genetics changed the scientific picture of Neanderthals. Evidence that they interbred with Homo sapiens, along with growing research into their behaviour, has shown that they were far more complex than earlier descriptions suggested.The rock crystal scraper became an early piece of evidence in that shift. It showed that Neanderthal technology was not simply about survival and efficiency, but could also involve decisions influenced by the appearance and character of materials.The Abri des Merveilles scraper remains a modest object in size, but its importance lies in the questions it raised. A single quartz tool forced archaeologists to reconsider assumptions about the minds behind prehistoric technology.The artefact’s careful shaping and unusual material choice provide a rare connection to the decisions of an individual Neanderthal craftsman thousands of years ago. Whether the stone was selected partly because of its beauty or simply because it was available, its existence shows that Neanderthal toolmaking involved thought, preference and a close relationship with the materials around them.Nearly 45,000 years later, the small piece of rock crystal continues to offer evidence of a more nuanced understanding of one of humanity’s closest extinct relatives.
Article Summary: 45,000-year-old Neanderthal quartz scraper highlights unusual stone tool technology in France. Tool, crafted from rare rock crystal, highlights that Neanderthals had an appreciation for aesthetics and craftsmanship. The sophistication in its creation suggests a deeper cultural understanding of their environment.

Article Title: Mapmakers created a one-square-metre “Null Island” at 0°N, 0°E, where missing or broken location data can appear
Article Text:
A weather buoy at 0° latitude, 0° longitude. Maintained by the PIRATA (Prediction and Research Moored Array in the Atlantic) project. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

How software defaults create

virtual geography

The figure shows the location of Null Island, a fictional place, at the intersection of the Equator and Prime Meridian, with geographic coordinates of (0°, 0°). Credits: Wikimedia Commons

Why Null Island matters for digital cartography

Every single day, many apps, delivery services, and weather portals can lose their way when location data is missing. When digital map databases encounter glitched, incomplete, or missing location coordinates, their internal software often falls back to zeros. This technical fallback can send that broken information to the intersection of the Equator and the Prime Meridian when missing coordinates default to zero. To help systems handle bad data, cartographers created a tiny virtual landmass at that spot, where misplaced location records can accumulate.According to the Library of Congress , mapping experts created a one-square-metre virtual feature at zero degrees north and zero degrees east within public datasets. Known informally as Null Island, this artificial landmass was added to handle broken code more smoothly. Located in the international waters of the Gulf of Guinea in the Atlantic Ocean, the site lies over deep open water, roughly 600 kilometres off the coast of West Africa. At this exact spot, oceanographers maintain the Soul buoy, an autonomous weather station managed by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration . The buoy measures surface marine conditions while surrounded by millions of phantom data check-ins.This strange phenomenon happens because software engineers often configure databases to treat empty location entries as zeros. According to the research published in IEEE Xplore , when mobile apps, shipping trackers, or IP-based tools fail to pinpoint a user’s true location, the system may fill the blank with zero degrees north and zero degrees east. As a result, many broken user check-ins, automated weather pings, and misformatted addresses can be mapped to this point in the ocean.The mechanism relies on simple computer programming logic in which zero acts as a neutral starting point in coordinate systems, but in mapmaking, zero degrees latitude and zero degrees longitude point to a real physical place on Earth. When an application fails to fetch satellite positioning data, the underlying database fills the missing values with zero rather than throwing an error message. The software treats these numerical zeros as precise geographic directions and plots the activity to the Gulf of Guinea. By placing a one-square-metre virtual island at those exact coordinates, cartographers gave these orphaned data points a safe place to land, helping digital maps stay working even when data gets scrambled.Data analysts say that traffic sent to Null Island can help monitor digital mapping networks. Monitoring sudden traffic spikes at these coordinates can help engineers spot glitched software updates, malfunctioning satellite receivers, and systematic errors in global address databases.The creation of Null Island highlights a major challenge in managing big data across global networks. As many connected devices constantly share location data, handling simple technical glitches cleanly has become essential for keeping everyday navigation tools reliable.As location-based services become increasingly woven into everyday life, from ride-hailing apps and food deliveries to weather forecasting and emergency response, even small errors in geographic coordinates can have wider consequences. A single default value may seem harmless, but when repeated across thousands or even millions of records, it can distort datasets, complicate research, and make technical problems harder to detect. Null Island has therefore become more than an internet curiosity, serving as a useful reminder of how seemingly minor software decisions can shape the way digital maps interpret the real world.This shows how software design interacts with real-world geography. Rather than letting mapping apps freeze when given invalid data, cartographers created a fallback location for invalid coordinates. Understanding how these computational defaults work can help database managers improve location tracking tools and explain where lost digital information goes when technology stumbles.
Article Summary: When digital map databases encounter glitched, incomplete, or missing location coordinates, their internal software often falls back to zeros. To help systems handle bad data, cartographers created a tiny virtual landmass at that spot, where misplaced location records can accumulate. Article Title: A livestream from Greenland’s UNESCO-listed Ilulissat Icefjord captured a mammoth iceberg rolling over and exposing its blue underside
Article Text:
Photo: MonaHansen1/ TikTok (Enhanced for clarity using AI)

What happened

Why icebergs flip

Ilulissat’s iceberg world

Why did the video go viral?

A reminder from the Arctic

A livestream from Greenland’s UNESCO-listed Ilulissat Icefjord caught one of nature’s most dramatic tricks: a mammoth iceberg slowly rolling over and exposing the blue underside that had been hidden below the waterline. The moment, filmed off the coast of Ilulissat on July 25, quickly spread online because it was both beautiful and strangely unsettling.The scale of the scene is part of what made it so striking. Ilulissat sits beside one of the most active glacier systems on Earth, where giant icebergs regularly break off, drift through the fjord and gradually reshape themselves as they melt and fracture in the Arctic water.The rollover was captured by a livestream camera near the entrance to Ilulissat Icefjord, with additional footage filmed by local residents. In the video, the iceberg appears to lean slowly before tipping decisively, sending waves across the surrounding water and exposing the rough, darker ice beneath the surface.Although the scene looked dramatic, no injuries or damage were reported. The iceberg remained offshore, far enough from the town that the event was more spectacle than danger.Icebergs do not stay perfectly balanced.Because roughly 90% of an iceberg lies underwater, uneven melting beneath the surface can shift its center of gravity until the ice can no longer remain upright.When that happens, it rolls or capsizes, releasing a burst of energy that churns the water and creates waves and mist.Experts say this is a natural process in Greenland, where icebergs are constantly changing shape as they drift. Large bergs can remain grounded near the mouth of the icefjord while they melt, fracture and become small enough to move on into Disko Bay.Ilulissat is often called the iceberg capital of the world, and the title is well earned. The town sits next to the Ilulissat Icefjord, a UNESCO World Heritage Site fed by Sermeq Kujalleq, one of the fastest-moving glaciers in the world. That glacier releases enormous amounts of ice into the sea, which is why dramatic bergs like this one are such a familiar part of local life.The region is also a reminder of a much bigger climate story. Greenland’s ice sheet is melting at an accelerating rate, contributing to sea-level rise around the world. So while a single iceberg rollover is a natural event, it is also part of a landscape that is changing under climate pressure.The footage was compelling because it captured something most of us will never get to see in person. The iceberg appears nearly sentient as it moves, then flips over with a ferocity that seems to dwarf the camera. That combination of grace and strength helped the clip spread quickly across social media. It also struck a chord with something more universal: our obsession with the unpredictable nature of the natural world. The flip was a reminder that icebergs are not fixed sculptures.They are constantly moving, melting and rebalancing in ways that are invisible until the moment they are not.For locals in Ilulissat, scenes like this are part of the rhythm of life in the Arctic. For the rest of the world, they offer a rare glimpse into a landscape where ice, ocean and climate are always in motion. The video may have looked like a stunt, but it was simply nature doing what nature does: on a spectacular scale.
Article Summary: The rollover was captured by a livestream camera near the entrance to Ilulissat Icefjord. In the video, the iceberg appears to lean slowly before tipping decisively. The video quickly spread online because it was both beautiful and strangely unsettling.

Article Title: Quote of the day by JS Mill: 'I have learned to seek my happiness by limiting my desires, rather than...' and the 19th-century cure for modern burnout
Article Text:
John Stuart Mill was a 19th-century philosopher who argued that true happiness comes from developing the mind

I have learned to seek my happiness by limiting my desires, rather than in attempting to satisfy them.”

The breakdown of a calculating mind

The utilitarian paradox

Curbing the engine of infinite wants

A shopper standing in the middle of a brightly lit superstore, holding three slightly different versions of the same household item, often feels an odd sense of confusion rather than freedom. The endless scroll of online stores promises that the perfect product to complete life is just one click away. Yet, as packages keep arriving at the door, the promised happiness often disappears, replaced by a lingering desire for whatever comes next.This cycle of endless consumption is exactly what the Victorian philosopher John Stuart Mill described when he wrote: “Mill’s observation completely changes the usual idea of finding happiness. Instead of seeing human desire as an endless list of needs that must be fulfilled, he argued that desire itself is what needs to be controlled. Satisfaction, in his view, does not come from building a bigger net to catch every passing impulse, but from reducing what we expect and demand from the world.John Stuart Mill published this reflection in his Autobiography in 1873, a book describing one of the most intense intellectual upbringings in Western history.Born in London in 1806, Mill was raised under a strict educational experiment designed by his father, James Mill, and the founder of Utilitarianism, Jeremy Bentham. By the age of three, he was learning Ancient Greek; by eight, he was reading Herodotus and Plato in their original language; and by his early teens, he had mastered political economy and formal logic.The purpose of this education was to create a perfectly rational follower of Bentham—a person trained to judge every action by calculating how to produce the greatest pleasure and the least pain for the greatest number of people.The experiment seemed successful until 1826, when twenty-year-old Mill suffered a serious mental breakdown. In one of the most famous parts of his memoir, Mill recalled asking himself a simple question: if all his political and social goals were achieved tomorrow, would he truly feel happy? His honest answer was an immediate “no.” His highly rational way of thinking had left him emotionally empty.Mill’s recovery happened gradually, helped by the poetry of William Wordsworth and by a major reconsideration of Utilitarian philosophy. He realized that Bentham’s basic idea—treating happiness as simply the total of fulfilled desires—was deeply incomplete. To recover his peace of mind, Mill had to rethink what true well-being meant. The quotation from his Autobiography marks this important turning point, showing his realization that lasting happiness comes from controlling desire rather than satisfying every new craving.To understand Mill’s change in thinking, we must examine a tension within Utilitarian philosophy. Traditional Utilitarianism viewed happiness as the total amount of pleasure minus pain. If people could continue creating and satisfying new desires, happiness should, in theory, continue increasing.Mill recognized the major problem with this idea: human desires constantly grow. As soon as one desire is fulfilled, our expectations rise again, a pattern that modern psychologists call the “hedonic treadmill.” Trying to find lasting happiness by satisfying every new want is like trying to fill a bucket full of holes.By encouraging people to limit their desires, Mill was not promoting extreme self-denial or the lifestyle of monks. Instead, he brought his updated version of Utilitarianism closer to older philosophical traditions. Epicurus had argued centuries earlier that simple, easily achieved pleasures bring the greatest peace of mind, while Stoic thinkers such as Seneca believed that true wealth comes not from owning many things, but from wanting fewer things.Mill adapted this idea for the modern industrial world. He argued that higher intellectual and emotional pleasures—such as art, friendship, public service, and personal development—are naturally more valuable than endlessly collecting material possessions. Limiting material and superficial desires frees mental energy, allowing people to develop deeper, non-material sources of happiness that do not lose their value once they are achieved.In 2026, Mill’s insight speaks directly to one of the biggest challenges of modern life: the commercialization of human attention and desire. Today’s digital systems are carefully designed to constantly create new wants that can only be satisfied through more consumption. Targeted algorithms, personalized advertising, and micro-influencers work together to convince people that something important is always missing from their lives.The growing popularity of voluntary simplicity, digital minimalism, and anti-consumption movements reflects Mill’s principle in action. When technology workers switch to basic feature phones or consumers commit to “no-buy” years, they are putting his idea into practice. They are not doing so because they lack money, but because they want to break the endless cycle of constantly creating new desires.The same principle also applies to work and professional burnout. Modern workplaces often define success through constant growth: higher salaries, bigger teams, and continuous promotions. However, research in behavioral economics consistently shows that once people reach a comfortable middle-class standard of living, extra income brings smaller and smaller increases in everyday happiness. Executives who reject promotions to protect their personal lives or professionals who choose lower-paying jobs for better health are deciding to reduce their ambitions rather than spend their lives chasing ever-growing demands.By describing happiness as the relationship between what people have and what they want, Mill offered a lasting mathematical insight: the result can be improved either by increasing what you have or by reducing what you want.When Mill died in Avignon in 1873, he left behind writings that influenced modern liberal democracy, individual freedom, and economic thought. Yet perhaps his greatest personal achievement was overcoming the crisis of his youth. By understanding that peace of mind depends on controlling desire instead of constantly feeding it, he left a timeless guide for staying mentally balanced in a world designed to keep people forever wanting more.
Article Summary: John Stuart Mill was a 19th-century philosopher who argued that true happiness comes from developing the mind. He argued that desire itself is what needs to be controlled. Limiting material and superficial desires frees mental energy, allowing people to develop deeper, non-material sources of happiness.

Article Title: In 2025, helicopters dropped 400 logs into Washington’s Pilchuck River: 28 engineered logjams now slow floodwaters and rebuild lost salmon habitat
Article Text:
Washington’s Pilchuck River | Wikimedia Commons

Washington’s Pilchuck River | Wikimedia Commons

Rivers once depended on fallen trees to stay healthy

Why helicopters were the only practical solution

A U.S. Army CH-47F | Wikimedia Commons

Restoring what rivers once built on their own

The roar of twin-rotor Chinook helicopters was heard all around Washington’s Pilchuck River valley in June 2025 as one massive log after another swung beneath cables toward the river below. It looked like an enormous logging operation from the air, while on the ground, crews were doing the opposite. Instead of clearing wood from the river, they were putting it back. Over several days, helicopters flew roughly 400 large logs into an eight-mile stretch of the Upper Pilchuck River, where they were assembled into 28 engineered logjams that were designed to recreate the tangled woody structures that once created Pacific Northwest rivers before decades of logging and flood-control work removed them. According to The Daily Herald, the effort is led by the Tulalip Tribes and the Washington State Department of Natural Resources as part of a long-term plan to restore habitat for threatened Chinook salmon while also trying to reduce erosion and slow floodwaters.A logjam might look like debris that should be removed to many people, but river scientists see something very different.Before widespread timber harvesting came into existence, large trees regularly toppled into rivers, where they redirected currents, trapped gravel, carved deep pools and created sheltered side channels. Those slow-moving pockets of water became nurseries for juvenile salmon, and offered protection from predators and strong winter flows. Many rivers were simplified into faster, straighter channels that carried water efficiently but left young fish with far fewer places to feed and grow. On the Pilchuck, the newly installed logjams are intended to reverse that process. The structures create a more complex river that benefits both fish and nearby communities by forcing water to spread across the floodplain and reconnect with historic side channels. Snohomish County states that engineered logjams also help reduce local erosion, increase floodplain connectivity, restore off-channel habitat and improve the river’s resilience during high-water events.Moving hundreds of logs into a remote river valley isn’t something conventional construction equipment can easily accomplish, since many restoration sites lie beyond existing roads or within sensitive habitats where heavy machinery would damage wetlands and riverbanks. Chinook helicopters solved that problem since each log could be lifted directly from staging areas and placed with remarkable precision, which allowed crews on the ground to anchor the wood into engineered structures without building new access routes. This approach also shortened construction time and reduced disturbance to surrounding forests. Seeing helicopters carry giant logs may appear unusual, but conservation agencies across the Pacific Northwest increasingly use aircraft when restoring rivers that are difficult to reach or environmentally sensitive. The Pilchuck project represents one of the region’s largest recent examples of aerial large-wood placement for salmon recovery.The Pilchuck River supports every species of Pacific salmon found in Washington, but populations have struggled as rivers have become warmer and disconnected from their floodplains. A watershed cannot be restored by simply reintroducing large wood, yet decades of restoration work have shown that engineered logjams can recreate many of the physical processes that healthy rivers once produced naturally. According to NOAA Fisheries , large woody structures slow water, create deeper pools, provide cover for juvenile salmon, and encourage rivers to develop the complex habitats that fish depend on throughout their life cycle. On the Pilchuck, the helicopters have already finished their work, but what remains is the slower process that cannot be rushed: allowing the river itself to reshape the logs, build new channels and, over time, become a place where young salmon have a better chance of surviving their journey to the Pacific Ocean.
Article Summary: The Pilchuck River in Washington was restored with the help of Chinook helicopters. Helicopters flew 400 large logs into an eight-mile stretch of the river. The logs were assembled into 28 engineered logjams that were designed to recreate the tangled woody structures that once created Pacific Northwest rivers.

Article Title: Scientists discover a new eyeless cavefish genus hidden for decades inside one of America's most closely monitored caves
Article Text:
Representative Image of the newly discovered Demon Cavefish in a dark underwater cave (Image of University of Alabama at Huntsville)

How a new genus went unnoticed inside a closely monitored cave

Why the fish's appearance made it so easy to overlook

What finally revealed the fish's true identity

Why cave ecosystems remain vulnerable despite being hard to reach

Why this discovery matters for how scientists study biodiversity

For more than three decades, biologists have carried out quarterly surveys of Bobcat Cave in northern Alabama, a site that sits beneath the secured grounds of the US Army's Redstone Arsenal and is already home to a well-known endangered species, the Alabama cave shrimp. After 30 years of closely monitored fieldwork in one of the most thoroughly documented cave ecosystems in North America, researchers have now identified an entirely new genus of eyeless cavefish quietly living in the same pools the whole time, hiding not through concealment but through an almost perfect physical resemblance to a completely unrelated species that shares its habitat.According to the University of Alabama in Huntsville, Bobcat Cave lies roughly eight miles from the university's campus, within the secured perimeter of Redstone Arsenal, a location that has effectively shielded the site from suburban development and given researchers unusually consistent long-term access to study its aquatic life. The cave has been surveyed on a quarterly basis for more than 30 years specifically to track the endangered Alabama cave shrimp, making it one of the more intensively studied subterranean ecosystems in the country.Amblyopsid cavefishes, the broader family this new species belongs to, have served as important model organisms for studying underground biology since the 1800s, and the freshwater fauna of eastern North America ranks among the most thoroughly catalogued in the world.Given that level of existing scrutiny, researchers have compared the discovery of an entirely new genus at this particular site to finding a new land mammal inside a well-studied national park, a discovery few expected was still possible.The reason this species escaped detection for so long comes down to a case of mistaken identity built on genuine biological convergence. According to Auburn University, the newly identified species, formally named Demogorgonichthys arcanus and commonly referred to as the Demon Cavefish, shares its pools with a previously known and well-documented neighbour, the Southern Cavefish, Typhlichthys subterraneus. Comparative genetic mapping confirmed that although both species have adapted to identical cave conditions, their genetic lineages actually branched apart from one another long ago, evolving independently rather than sharing a recent common ancestor.Through a process known as convergent evolution, in which unrelated species independently develop similar physical traits in response to similar environmental pressures, both fish separately evolved pale, colourless skin and lost functional eyesight, adaptations well suited to a life spent entirely in complete darkness. Because the underground environment shaped both species into such closely matching outward appearances, generations of field surveyors had simply grouped the two lookalike fish together during routine population counts, never suspecting that two genetically distinct genera were swimming in the same pools all along.Uncovering the truth required moving well beyond a simple visual identification in the field. According to the University of Alabama in Huntsville, researchers turned to detailed anatomical examination, high-resolution CT scanning and genetic sequencing to properly characterise the newly noticed specimens. This deeper analysis revealed distinct skeletal structures separating the Demon Cavefish from its Southern Cavefish neighbour, along with a telling genetic clue: a nonfunctional, or vestigial, light-sensing rhodopsin gene, evidence of a fish whose ancestors once relied on eyesight before evolving in complete darkness, eventually rendering that gene obsolete.Researchers also suspect the Demon Cavefish spends much of its life in deeper, largely inaccessible aquifer channels beneath the cave, surfacing into the more visible and regularly surveyed pools of Bobcat Cave only occasionally, a pattern that would help explain why it remained so difficult to reliably distinguish from its more commonly documented neighbour across three decades of quarterly monitoring.Even though Bobcat Cave's location within a secured military installation has helped protect it from direct human disturbance, researchers note that cave pools like these remain closely linked to the surface through groundwater systems. This connection means agricultural runoff, surface sediment and chemical contaminants originating miles away can still make their way into these subterranean pools, posing an ongoing threat to species that, in many cases, exist nowhere else on Earth.According to thestudy Surprising cryptic cavefish diversity in a long-studied karst cave ecosystem of northern Alabama , protecting cryptic, highly specialised cave species like the Demon Cavefish ultimately requires safeguarding entire surface recharge basins rather than simply restricting physical access to a cave entrance, since the health of these hidden ecosystems depends heavily on water quality far beyond the cave's own boundaries.The discovery of Demogorgonichthys arcanus stands as a reminder that even ecosystems studied intensively for decades can still conceal entirely unknown branches of the evolutionary tree, particularly when convergent evolution produces close physical lookalikes that easily fool visual identification in the field. For researchers working to protect North Alabama's cave systems, the finding underscores that thorough, long-running monitoring programmes remain essential, not only for tracking known species but for eventually revealing biodiversity that has been quietly present, and quietly overlooked, the entire time.
Article Summary: New genus of eyeless cavefish found living in same pools for 30 years. Discovered in Bobcat Cave in northern Alabama, a site that sits beneath the secured grounds of the US Army's Redstone Arsenal. The newly identified species, formally named Demogorgonichthys arcanus, shares its pools with a previously known and well-documented neighbour, Typhlichthys subterraneus.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:
Your credit score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity.

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.
Article Summary: Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.

Article Title: Before the knowledge walks out the door
Article Text:
Everyone in Silicon Valley is racing to build machines that replace human expertise.

Ahmer Inam

, a schoolteacher's son from Delhi, is building machines that inherit it.

When Ahmer Inam appeared on Fox & Friends in June, his mother watched the segment without following much of it. Her English is limited. There was her son on the famous curved couch of American morning television, fielding questions about artificial intelligence, and she understood almost none of the words. She wept anyway. Some distances need no translation, and the one between a schoolteacher's household in Delhi and a Manhattan television studio is legible in any language.Had she followed the argument, it might have surprised her less than it surprised the audience. Because what Inam was defending, underneath the vocabulary of frontier AI, is approximately the oldest idea in civilisation — the one his father practised for a living: that knowledge survives only when one generation troubles to hand it to the next.Inam has spent twenty-five years building artificial intelligence — long enough to remember when it meant symbolic logic in the late nineties, and senior enough to have run AI and data for Fortune 500 companies, Nike and Wells Fargo among them, back when "chief AI officer" was still an exotic title. He is not, in other words, a critic sniping from the cheap seats. Which makes the thesis of Cognisee, the research lab he founded and leads, sound almost seditious in today's Silicon Valley: "We're not trying to replace the worker," he says."We're trying to make the worker irreplaceable."The problem he is aiming at usually gets filed under the bland heading of "labour shortage." By one estimate, more than two million skilled-trade jobs in the United States could sit unfilled by 2030 — electricians, welders, machinists, the hands America needs if it is serious about building factories, chip plants and grid capacity again. But Inam's diagnosis is sharper than a headcount. "America does not have a work shortage," he likes to say. "It has an expertise shortage."Consider what actually leaves the building when a master electrician retires at sixty-eight. Not the manual — the manual stays. What leaves is the ear that catches a motor running slightly wrong two weeks before it fails; the instinct that connects a faint vibration to a pattern in old maintenance logs; forty years of judgment that was never written down because it could not be. The philosopher Michael Polanyi had a name for this — tacit knowledge, the things we know but cannot tell — and Cognisee is, at bottom, a bet that the most valuable training data on earth is tacit.The company's method has a fable-like symmetry. Its AI begins as an apprentice: it works alongside experienced people and learns what they notice, what they ask, how they make judgment calls. Then it turns around and becomes a coach, carrying that accumulated judgment to the newcomer. "First it's an apprentice," Inam says. "Then it becomes a coach." Picture a 22-year-old on his first aircraft-maintenance job, hearing a sound he has never heard before, with the distilled instincts of the country's best technicians beside him in real time. "He's not being replaced by a machine," Inam says. "He's being mentored by one."The repository where all this lives is called, a little grandly, a Wisdom Vault — a secure library of hard-won know-how from doctors, nurses, electricians, factory workers, farmers, small-business owners. Grand or not, the name gives away the emotional register Inam is working in. This is not pitched as workforce optimisation. It is pitched as inheritance.He is careful — insistent, actually — about the question that framing invites: who owns it? In Cognisee's design, the expert decides what to preserve, what to share, and with whom; the contributor is recognised and rewarded; the knowledge belongs to the person who earned it, not to the machine that absorbed it. "There is a big difference," Inam says, "between being monitored and being mentored." The company is incorporated as a public benefit corporation, which he describes as a legal commitment to the worker rather than a marketing pledge.That ownership principle is also where his quarrel with the reigning AI paradigm becomes explicit. The frontier labs, Inam argues, got intelligent by swallowing the written internet — and the written internet is now substantially swallowed, which is why the industry's plan increasingly amounts to bigger data centres and more electricity, even as some of the field's own pioneers warn of a wall ahead. His contrarian wager is that the next leap will come not from more compute but from the knowledge that never made it onto the internet in the first place — and that it can be gathered by consent rather than by crawler.For an Indian reader, the resonance is hard to miss. This is a country that has watched its weaves, its remedies and its craft knowledge catalogued, carried off and sold back to it before. It is also a country whose deepest teaching traditions were never textual at all, but moved from person to person — the guru-shishya parampara, the ustad and the shagird. Inam has spoken about Wisdom Vaults for indigenous and medicinal knowledge, with communities retaining ownership of what they contribute. One way to describe Cognisee is as an attempt to give the world's oral inheritances an infrastructure layer — sovereignty included.The idea is attracting converts from unexpected quarters. Cognisee's co-founder, Alex Giannou, spent nearly two decades on Wall Street financing precisely the data centres and power deals behind the AI boom; he crossed over, in Inam's telling, because the right bet and the smart bet turned out to be the same one. Among the company's early backers is a senior Google executive who helped invent federated learning, one of the foundational privacy-preserving techniques of modern machine learning. And last year the XPRIZE Foundation, where Inam serves as a Visionary, recognised his work with its Global Visioneering Award.None of which quite explains the conviction. For that you have to go back to Delhi. Inam grew up in a low-income household, the son of a teacher — a man who spent his working life on the least scalable expertise-transfer technology ever devised: one adult, one room, one generation at a time. The son's journey to America was not gilded; there were stretches, early on, when he could not always afford to eat. It takes a particular kind of person to emerge from that and conclude that a nation's most undervalued asset sits not in its server farms but in the heads of its retiring machinists and nurses."Every generation should start where the last one left off," Inam says. It sounds like a product principle. It is closer to a family creed — the thing his father practised without ever calling it a thesis, the thing his mother recognised on a television screen in a language she does not speak. Some knowledge, it turns out, transfers just fine.
Article Summary: Ahmer Inam, a schoolteacher's son from Delhi, is building machines that inherit it. The problem he is aiming at usually gets filed under the bland heading of "labour shortage" By one estimate, more than two million skilled-trade jobs in the United States could sit unfilled by 2030.

Article Title: Twitter product head resigns, sends thanks note to Elon Musk and team; Tesla CEO responds
Article Text:
Nikita Bier thanked Elon Musk and team



Tesla CEO Elon Musk responds to Nikita Bier’s post



Read Nikita Bier’s complete post here



Ladies and gentlemen, it's time to pass the torch and demote myself to my natural state: a poster. I'll be stepping back from leading product for 𝕏 and will continue on as an advisor.

Serving the X community has been the privilege of a lifetime. X is, and will remain, the most important communication technology in history. But running this app is a 24/7 job and it's now time for me to take a breather.

Nikita Bier, the product head at X (formerly known as Twitter) has stepped down from his position after serving in the role for just over a year.
